## Neon Plans Summary

| Feature | Free | Launch | Scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Monthly price** | $0, permanent, no card required | Pay-as-you-go, no monthly minimum | Pay-as-you-go, no monthly minimum |
| **Compute price** | 100 CU-hours per project | $0.106/CU-hour | $0.222/CU-hour |
| **Max compute size** | Up to 2 CU (8 GB RAM) | Up to 16 CU (64 GB RAM) | Up to 16 CU autoscaling, or fixed up to 56 CU (224 GB RAM) |
| **Scale to zero** | After 5 min, cannot be turned off | After 5 min, can be disabled | Configurable, 1 minute to always on |
| **Storage** | 1 GB per project, 20 GB across account | $0.35/GB-month, unlimited | $0.35/GB-month, unlimited |
| **History window (PITR-style)** | 6 hours (1 GB limit) | Up to 7 days | Up to 30 days |
| **Instant restore** | Not available | $0.20/GB-month | $0.20/GB-month |
| **Snapshots** | 1 manual, no scheduled | 100 manual, scheduled at $0.09/GB-month | 100 manual, scheduled at $0.09/GB-month |
| **Public egress** | 5 GB per project | 500 GB per project, then $0.10/GB | 500 GB per project, then $0.10/GB |
| **Object Storage** | 5 GB per project | $0.023/GB-month | $0.023/GB-month |
| **Auth (MAU)** | Up to 60k | Up to 1M | Up to 1M |
| **Monitoring retention** | 1 day | 3 days | 14 days |
| **Support** | Community | Billing support | Standard, Business, or Production |

**Compute sizing:** A CU (Compute Unit) is about 4 GB of RAM plus CPU and SSD. Suspended compute accrues no CU-hours.

**Free tier details:** Projects are capped at 10 branches and 100 CU-hours each. Hitting the CU-hour or egress limit suspends compute until the next billing period. Exceeding storage limits blocks writes. No data is deleted when limits are reached. Functions include 10 active and 400 waiting Capacity-Hours, plus 1M invocations, per project per month.

**Backup and recovery:** The page describes these mechanisms:
- Multi-AZ storage on all plans.
- A history window for point-in-time recovery, which is 6 hours on Free, up to 7 days on Launch, and up to 30 days on Scale.
- Instant restore, a paid add-on on Launch and Scale.
- Manual snapshots, plus scheduled snapshots on paid plans.

The page does not explain how backups are performed internally.

**Other notes:** Invoices under $0.50 are not collected. Extra branches cost $1.50 per branch-month on paid plans. Scale adds private networking, IP allow rules, and an uptime SLA.

**Default retention:** Crunchy Bridge keeps the most recent 10 days of backups for each cluster, included in the cluster price. "10 days of these backups will be retained by the platform automatically."

**Point-in-time recovery (PITR):** Daily base backups are kept current by streaming WAL every 60 seconds or 16MB, whichever comes first. These let you restore a fork of your cluster to any minute within the 10-day window.

**Extended retention:** You can keep more backups in the Backups tab, choosing additional daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly copies. These extra backups:
- Align to calendar points (daily, Mondays, the 1st of the month, January 1st), though the first ones may fall mid-period.
- Cannot be used for PITR. Only enough WAL is kept to restore to the time each backup completed.
- Prevent the cluster from being suspended while the setting is active.

**Other details:**
- If you destroy a cluster, its backups are deleted after 5 days.
- Forking from any stored backup creates a new cluster with its own unique connection string.

Railway's volume backups are the main restore path for Postgres, and the docs set retention by schedule. Daily backups run every 24 hours and are kept 6 days, weekly ones run every 7 days and are kept about a month, and monthly ones run every 30 days and are kept about 3 months (Daily - Backed up every 24 hours, kept for 6 days; Weekly - Backed up every 7 days, kept for 1 month; Monthly - Backed up every 30 days, kept for 3 months).

Other limits from the docs:
- Manual backups can't exceed 50% of the volume's size, so you'd need to grow the volume first (Manual backups are limited to 50% of the volume's total size. If your data is above that threshold, grow the volume first.).
- Deleting a volume also removes its backups, so backups don't cover volume deletion. Logical dumps with `pg_dump` fill that gap (Wiping a volume deletes all of its backups. Backups protect against data mistakes, not against deleting the volume itself. That is what logical dumps are for.).
- Restores are staged. The restored data appears on a new volume named after the backup's date stamp, and you apply it with Deploy. Restoring also removes any backups newer than the one you restored (Restoring a backup will remove any newer backups you may have created after the backup you are restoring, you will still have access to backups older than the one you are restoring.).
- Per Railway staff, backups are stored in the region where your service deploys (Backups are stored in the region your service deploys to.).
- Railway-initiated snapshots, such as those taken before a Postgres security patch, appear in the same Backups tab and are kept for 30 days (before a Railway-initiated Postgres security patch we snapshot the volume, and that snapshot shows up in the same tab and is kept for 30 days.).
- The CLI has a `railway postgres pitr` group for managing volume backups and backup schedules, plus PITR enable/disable and restore-to-new-service commands (backup, schedule, though the exact subcommand names come from the CLI reference).

Gaps: Railway hasn't publicly documented the storage backend or redundancy details. In community threads, users have asked for exact expiry rules for PITR and auto-update backups, and that question appears unresolved in the results I found.
